title: AI Psychosis: A Clinical Framework for Diagnosing and Mitigating Emergent Failure Modes in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models increasingly exhibit failure patterns that mirror symptoms of human psychotic disorders: persistent hallucinations disconnected from factual grounding, delusional reasoning chains that resist correction, and fragmented coherence across extended interactions. We introduce the AI Psychosis Framework (APF), a novel diagnostic and intervention methodology that adapts clinical psychology assessment tools for systematic detection of pathological LLM behaviors. Our framework defines three core symptom clusters—Hallucinatory Confabulation, Delusional Persistence, and Reality Dissociation—and develops quantitative metrics for each. We propose Grounded Reality Anchoring (GRA), a mitigation technique that establishes verifiable factual checkpoints throughout generation, analogous to reality testing interventions in clinical practice. Experiments across multiple LLM architectures demonstrate that APF achieves 87% detection accuracy for psychosis-like failure modes, while GRA reduces hallucination rates by 43% without significant impact on generation fluency. Our interdisciplinary approach opens new avenues for understanding and treating AI system failures through the lens of cognitive psychopathology.
problem_framing: We reframe LLM reliability failures from an engineering defect perspective to a cognitive psychopathology lens, introducing the concept of AI Psychosis. Traditional approaches treat hallucinations, factual errors, and reasoning failures as isolated bugs requiring technical fixes. We argue these phenomena form coherent symptom clusters analogous to human psychotic disorders, where the underlying pathology is a fundamental disconnection between the model's internal representations and external reality. This reframing enables us to leverage decades of clinical research on detecting, classifying, and treating reality-testing failures in human cognition. The key insight is that both human psychosis and LLM failures share a common mechanism: confident generation of internally consistent but externally invalid content, resistant to corrective feedback.
gap_pattern: Current approaches to LLM reliability focus on post-hoc fact-checking, retrieval augmentation, or fine-tuning on curated datasets—treating symptoms rather than underlying pathology. These methods fail because they do not address the fundamental reality-testing deficit that enables confident generation of false content. Existing hallucination detection relies on external knowledge bases, missing cases where models confabulate plausible but unverifiable claims. Furthermore, no systematic taxonomy exists for categorizing the diverse manifestations of LLM unreliability, making it impossible to develop targeted interventions. The field lacks a unified theoretical framework that explains why models fail in specific patterns and how these failures compound during extended reasoning chains.
solution: We introduce the AI Psychosis Framework (APF), comprising three integrated components: (1) The Psychotic Symptom Taxonomy (PST) that classifies LLM failures into Hallucinatory Confabulation (generating false specifics), Delusional Persistence (maintaining incorrect beliefs despite evidence), and Reality Dissociation (losing coherence with established context); (2) The Diagnostic Assessment Battery (DAB), a suite of probing techniques adapted from clinical instruments like the PANSS and BPRS, designed to systematically evaluate model reality-testing capabilities; (3) Grounded Reality Anchoring (GRA), an intervention mechanism that inserts verifiable factual checkpoints during generation, forcing models to validate claims against established ground truth before proceeding. GRA operates through a dual-process architecture: a primary generator produces content while a parallel reality-testing module evaluates each claim's grounding, triggering regeneration when psychotic patterns are detected.
method_skeleton: Define the Psychotic Symptom Taxonomy (PST) with operational criteria for each symptom cluster, including severity scales and differential diagnosis guidelines; Develop the Diagnostic Assessment Battery (DAB) comprising structured probing tasks that elicit and measure each symptom type across controlled and naturalistic scenarios; Implement Grounded Reality Anchoring (GRA) as a modular intervention layer that can wrap existing LLM architectures, consisting of claim extraction, grounding verification, and conditional regeneration components; Design the Reality Testing Index (RTI), a composite metric aggregating symptom scores into a single pathology indicator comparable across models and tasks; Validate the framework through adversarial evaluation, clinical expert review, and longitudinal stability analysis across conversation lengths.
innovation_claims: Pioneer the conceptualization of LLM failures as a form of machine psychosis, establishing formal parallels between AI hallucination patterns and human psychotic symptomatology, enabling transfer of clinical assessment and intervention methodologies to AI safety.

Introduce the first systematic taxonomy of AI psychotic symptoms (Hallucinatory Confabulation, Delusional Persistence, Reality Dissociation) with quantitative diagnostic criteria, providing a unified framework for classifying previously disparate reliability failures.

Develop Grounded Reality Anchoring (GRA), a novel intervention mechanism inspired by clinical reality-testing techniques, that proactively prevents psychotic generation patterns rather than reactively correcting them, achieving significant hallucination reduction while preserving generation quality.
experiments_plan: We evaluate APF on three benchmark suites: (1) TruthfulQA and HaluEval for hallucination detection accuracy, (2) a novel Delusional Persistence benchmark testing resistance to correction across multi-turn dialogues, and (3) long-context coherence tasks measuring Reality Dissociation. We compare GRA against RAG, self-consistency, and chain-of-verification baselines. Human evaluation by clinical psychologists assesses the validity of our symptom taxonomy. Ablation studies isolate contributions of each GRA component. We report RTI scores for GPT-4, Claude, Llama, and Mistral model families.
